# Rack Module for Stacking Medical Product Administration Devices

## Field of the Invention

The present invention relates to a rack module designed for stacking with at least one other identical or complementary module in order to form a support column, commonly referred to as a rack, intended to accommodate and support medical product administration devices. Such racks are typically used in hospital or clinical environments where multiple infusion pumps, syringe drivers, or similar devices must be organized, powered, and connected to a data network in a compact and efficient manner.

## General Description of the Rack Module

Each rack module according to the invention comprises at least one dedicated site equipped with a plug configured to simultaneously provide electric current supply and data transfer capability to a medical product administration device connected at that site. This dual-functionality plug ensures that, once a device is mounted onto the module, it receives the necessary power to operate while also being integrated into a communication network, allowing for centralized monitoring, control, and data exchange with hospital information systems or dedicated software applications.

In order to enable multiple modules to be assembled together to form a complete rack, each module is further provided with an inlet connector and an outlet connector. These two connectors are electrically and communicatively linked within the module via internal power lines and data transfer lines, ensuring continuity of both electrical supply and data communication throughout the entire stacked assembly. When several modules are stacked on top of one another, the outlet connector of one module engages with the inlet connector of the adjacent module, thereby establishing an uninterrupted chain of power and data connections along the full height of the rack.

## The Mobile Connector Innovation

A particularly advantageous and inventive feature of the present rack module lies in the design and behavior of its connectors. Specifically, either the inlet connector or the outlet connector—designated herein as the "mobile connector"—is configured to be movable between two distinct positions: a stocking position and a connected position. The remaining connector, referred to as the "second connector," remains fixed in place and does not exhibit this mobility.

In its stocking position, the mobile connector is retracted or otherwise positioned so as to be protected from external contact, impact, or interference, which is particularly beneficial during handling, transport, or storage of the module prior to its assembly into a rack. When the module is to be connected to an adjacent module to form part of the stacked column, the mobile connector can be displaced into its connected position, where it engages properly with the corresponding connector of the neighboring module, thereby establishing the required electrical and data connection.

## Advantages of the Mobile Connector Design

This innovative arrangement, wherein one of the two connectors is movable while the other remains stationary, offers several significant advantages over conventional rack module designs. Firstly, by allowing the mobile connector to be safely stored in a protected stocking position when not in use, the risk of accidental damage to the connector—such as bending of pins, contamination of contacts, or breakage of connector housings—is substantially reduced. This is especially important in demanding clinical environments where modules may be frequently handled, transported between departments, or temporarily disconnected for maintenance or reconfiguration purposes.

Secondly, the mobile connector design simplifies the overall process of connecting and stacking rack modules. Because the mobile connector can be moved into its connected position only when needed, users benefit from a more intuitive and controlled assembly procedure, reducing the likelihood of misalignment or improper connection during stacking. This not only enhances the reliability of the electrical and data connections within the rack but also contributes to a more user-friendly and efficient setup process for healthcare personnel who may need to quickly assemble or modify rack configurations according to clinical needs.

Overall, the combination of a fixed second connector and a movable mobile connector represents a practical and elegant solution to the challenges associated with the handling, protection, and interconnection of rack modules, thereby improving both the durability and usability of rack systems designed for medical product administration devices.

# Modular Connection System for Stackable Medical Rack Modules

## Field of the Invention

The present invention relates to the field of medical equipment infrastructure, and more particularly to systems and mechanisms for interconnecting stackable rack modules used in the construction of support columns for medical administration devices. These support columns are commonly employed in clinical settings to organize and power infusion pumps, monitoring equipment, and other bedside medical devices while providing integrated data communication pathways between stacked units.

## Background of the Invention

Modern healthcare facilities increasingly rely on modular rack systems that allow multiple medical administration devices to be stacked vertically, forming a single integrated support column. This modular approach offers significant advantages in terms of space efficiency, cable management, and workflow optimization at the patient bedside. Each rack module in such a system typically incorporates both power and data connectors, enabling seamless transmission of electrical power and digital information between adjacent modules once they are assembled into a column.

However, a persistent challenge in the design of these modular systems has been the vulnerability of the electrical and data connectors during periods when the modules are not assembled—specifically during storage, transport, and handling prior to installation. Traditional rack module designs feature connectors that remain in a fixed, exposed position at all times, regardless of whether the module is connected to an adjacent unit or standing alone. This constant exposure creates substantial risk of physical damage to the connector pins, contacts, or housing through accidental impacts, dust ingress, moisture exposure, or improper handling during the module's lifecycle outside of its assembled state.

Furthermore, conventional fixed-connector designs often complicate the assembly process itself, requiring careful alignment of multiple exposed contact points simultaneously, which can be cumbersome for clinical staff who may need to reconfigure rack systems quickly in time-sensitive healthcare environments.

## Summary of the Invention

To address these shortcomings, the present invention introduces a novel connector architecture for stackable rack modules that incorporates a **movable "mobile connector"** capable of transitioning between two distinct operational positions: a **stocking position** and a **connected position**. This mobile connector works in conjunction with a **fixed "second connector"** located on the corresponding face of an adjacent module, together forming the complete electrical and data interface between stacked units.

In the stocking position, the mobile connector is retracted or otherwise repositioned away from the exposed exterior surface of the rack module, effectively shielding its sensitive contact elements from external forces, contaminants, and accidental contact during storage or transport. This protective configuration is the default state of the module whenever it is not actively joined to an adjacent unit in a support column.

When two rack modules are brought together for assembly, the mobile connector is displaced from its stocking position into its connected position, where it engages directly with the second, fixed connector on the neighboring module. This engagement establishes the necessary electrical power pathway and data communication link between the two units, allowing the assembled column to function as an integrated system.

## Detailed Description

The mobile connector may be implemented through various mechanical arrangements, including but not limited to sliding mechanisms, rotating or pivoting assemblies, or spring-loaded extension mechanisms, any of which permit controlled movement between the two defined positions. The transition between the stocking and connected positions may be actuated manually by the user during the assembly process, or it may be designed to occur automatically as a consequence of the physical act of stacking one module atop another—for instance, through a cam mechanism or guided track that translates the mechanical force of module engagement into connector displacement.

The fixed second connector, by contrast, remains stationary and does not require repositioning, serving as a stable receiving interface for the mobile connector during the connection process. This asymmetric design—featuring one movable and one fixed connector—simplifies the alignment requirements during assembly, as clinical or technical staff need only properly position and displace the single mobile connector rather than manipulate multiple moving parts simultaneously.

## Advantages of the Invention

This connector architecture yields several important benefits over traditional fixed-connector designs:

1. **Enhanced Protection During Storage and Handling**: By allowing the mobile connector to retreat into a stocking position when not in use, the invention substantially reduces the likelihood of damage from impacts, debris, or moisture that might otherwise compromise the connector's functionality.

2. **Extended Equipment Lifespan**: Reduced exposure to physical stress and environmental contaminants translates into improved durability and reliability of the connection interface over repeated cycles of assembly, disassembly, and storage.

3. **Simplified Assembly Process**: The single-connector movement design streamlines the process of joining rack modules, reducing the complexity and potential for user error during column assembly in busy clinical environments.

4. **Improved Safety**: Minimizing exposed, potentially damaged electrical contacts reduces risks associated with electrical faults, short circuits, or improper connections that could otherwise compromise the safe operation of connected medical administration devices.

5. **Cost Efficiency**: By decreasing the incidence of connector damage and the associated need for repair or replacement, the invention contributes to lower long-term maintenance costs for healthcare facilities utilizing modular rack systems.

## Conclusion

The invention thus provides a practical and effective solution to the longstanding problem of connector vulnerability in stackable medical rack module systems. By introducing a mobile connector capable of shifting between protective and operational positions, in cooperation with a fixed second connector on adjacent modules, the design achieves a meaningful reduction in damage risk while simultaneously easing the burden of module assembly for end users in medical settings.

# The, This

The words we use to point at things reveal how we think about reality itself. "This" and "the" are among the smallest words in English, yet they carry enormous weight in how we construct meaning.

"This" is a word of immediacy. It reaches out and touches something—an object, an idea, a moment—and says: *here, now, close to me*. When we say "this book" or "this feeling," we're not just identifying something; we're placing ourselves in relation to it. This word requires context. It cannot exist in isolation, because "this" only makes sense when there is a speaker, a listener, and something shared between them in the present moment.

"The" works differently, though it too depends on shared understanding. "The" is the word of specificity within a known set. When I say "the door," I'm not referring to just any door, but a particular one that you and I both understand from context—perhaps the only door in the room, or the one we've already been discussing. "The" assumes a kind of common ground has already been established.

Together, these small words do enormous cognitive work. They are among the first grammatical tools children learn to wield, not because they carry rich meaning on their own, but because they organize the world into what is known, shared, and present versus what is general or abstract.

In this sense, "the" and "this" are less about naming things and more about relationships—between speaker and listener, between the said and the unsaid, between the specific and the general. They remind us that language is never just about objects in the world; it's about how we navigate that world together, pointing, sharing, and building common understanding one small word at a time.

# ABSTRACT

A stackable rack module system for holding and interconnecting medical infusion devices is disclosed. The system comprises a plurality of individual rack modules, each configured to removably receive and secure at least one medical infusion device, such as an infusion pump. Each module includes a housing having complementary mechanical interlocking features disposed on upper and lower surfaces, enabling multiple modules to be vertically stacked and securely coupled to form a modular tower configuration of variable height. Each module further incorporates at least one electrical connector and at least one data connector positioned to automatically mate with corresponding connectors on an adjacent module upon stacking, thereby establishing a continuous power distribution bus and a communication data bus across the assembled stack without requiring separate external cabling between modules. The electrical connector arrangement is configured to supply operating power from a common power source to each infusion device secured within the stack, while the data connector arrangement enables bidirectional transmission of operational data, alarm signals, and device status information between individual modules and to a central control or monitoring unit. The modular architecture allows for scalable configuration, hot-swappable module addition or removal, and simplified maintenance, while reducing cable clutter and connection errors in clinical environments. A locking mechanism may be provided to secure the mechanical and electrical connections between adjacent modules, ensuring reliable engagement during patient care use. The system may further include indicator lights, module identification circuitry, and fail-safe disconnect features to enhance safety and traceability of connected infusion devices within a clinical setting.

counterfactuals.output:
# Modular Hospital Equipment Rack System with Impact-Resistant Movable Connectors

## Technical Field

This invention relates to modular equipment mounting systems for medical environments, specifically to hospital equipment racks incorporating floating or movable inlet/outlet connector assemblies designed to absorb mechanical stress during transport, docking, and routine handling.

## Background

Hospital equipment racks house critical devices—infusion pumps, monitors, ventilator interfaces, gas manifolds, and power distribution units—that require frequent connection and disconnection as racks are relocated between patient rooms, storage bays, and service areas. Conventional fixed-connector designs suffer from a persistent failure mode: rigid mounting of inlet/outlet ports causes connector pins, housings, and internal PCB traces to bear the full shock load whenever racks are bumped, rolled over thresholds, or misaligned during docking. This results in cracked housings, bent pins, intermittent electrical faults, and costly connector replacement, often during time-critical clinical use.

## Summary of the Invention

The invention provides a modular hospital equipment rack architecture in which inlet and outlet connectors are mounted on **floating carriages** rather than fixed panel positions. Each connector module is suspended within a compliant housing that permits limited translational and rotational movement (typically 2–5 mm linear travel, ±3–5° angular deflection) before contact is made with a rigid stop. This movement is engineered to absorb misalignment and impact energy that would otherwise transmit directly to the electrical or fluidic interface.

## Detailed Description

### 1. Rack Module Architecture

The system comprises individual rack modules of standardized height/width (per ISO/IEC equipment rail conventions, e.g., 3U/6U increments) that stack or side-mount to form a composite rack assembly. Each module contains:

- A structural frame (extruded aluminum or reinforced polymer)
- One or more **connector carriage assemblies** at the module's mating face
- Internal wiring/tubing with strain-relief service loops sized to accommodate carriage travel

### 2. Floating Connector Carriage

Each inlet/outlet connector (electrical, data, pneumatic, or fluidic) is mounted not directly to the rack chassis but to a carriage plate that rides within a housing cavity on one of the following compliance mechanisms:

- **Elastomeric bushing suspension**: silicone or polyurethane grommets (Shore A 40–60) surrounding mounting posts, permitting omnidirectional float
- **Spring-loaded gimbal mount**: a two-axis gimbal with compression springs providing centering force and rotational compliance
- **Sliding dovetail rail with damped return**: linear travel along one axis with a viscoelastic damper preventing connector overshoot

The carriage is captured by a rigid outer housing with mechanical stops that limit maximum travel, preventing over-extension of internal conductors or hoses while still allowing sufficient deflection to absorb impact energy before it reaches the connector pins or seals.

### 3. Self-Aligning Mating Geometry

To complement the floating mechanism, connector faces incorporate:

- Chamfered or conical guide leads on both male and female halves
- Optional magnetic or spring-detent centering assist for blind-mate connections
- Keying features preventing cross-connection between dissimilar service types (e.g., medical air vs. suction)

This geometry allows the floating connector to self-correct minor misalignment (up to several degrees or millimeters) during docking, rather than forcing pins into a jammed or off-axis mating condition.

### 4. Strain Relief and Service Loop Management

Because the connector carriage moves relative to the fixed chassis, internal cabling and tubing include a **service loop** of defined slack, routed through a low-friction guide channel or cable chain. This prevents the floating motion from placing tensile or flexural stress on solder joints, crimped terminals, or barbed fluidic fittings.

### 5. Impact Detection (Optional Embodiment)

An additional embodiment incorporates a microswitch or Hall-effect sensor at the carriage's maximum-travel stop, allowing the rack's control electronics to log impact events exceeding a threshold displacement—supporting predictive maintenance and damage audit trails.

## Advantages

- Reduces connector and PCB damage from routine transport shocks
- Extends service life of high-cycle-count connectors (power, network, medical gas)
- Enables faster, error-tolerant docking in time-sensitive clinical settings
- Reduces unplanned downtime and replacement part costs
- Compatible with standard modular rack form factors, enabling retrofit

## Alternative Embodiments

- Application to mobile equipment carts and headwall units, not solely fixed racks
- Use of pneumatic (air-cushioned) float mechanisms in place of springs/elastomers
- Integration with quick-release module bays where the entire connector block, not just the carriage, is field-replaceable

---

*This description is drafted in general technical/patent-application style and would typically be accompanied by claims, drawings (exploded views of carriage assembly, cross-sections of gimbal/spring mechanisms), and reference numerals in an actual filing.*

# Patent Draft: Rack Module for Medical Device Administration Units

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates generally to modular medical device systems, and more particularly to a rack-mountable module architecture for medical administration units having interconnecting power and data communication pathways between vertically stacked modules, including a retractable connector assembly for facilitating selective engagement and disengagement of adjacent modules.

## BACKGROUND

Medical administration units, such as infusion pump systems, syringe drivers, and multi-channel delivery devices, are frequently deployed in stacked or racked configurations to enable simultaneous therapy delivery to a single patient or across multiple patients within a clinical setting. Conventional stacking arrangements often require separate cabling for power distribution and data communication between individual modules, resulting in cable management challenges, increased points of failure, and elevated risk of inadvertent disconnection during patient transport or module servicing.

There exists a need in the art for a rack module architecture that provides integrated power and data interconnection between adjacently stacked modules while minimizing exposed connector surfaces and reducing the risk of connector damage or contamination during handling.

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

In one aspect, the present disclosure provides a rack module for a medical device administration system comprising a housing defining a top surface and a bottom surface, the housing configured to mechanically interlock with at least one additional rack module in a vertically stacked arrangement. The module further comprises a power transfer interface and a data transfer interface disposed at the top surface and/or bottom surface, the interfaces configured to establish electrical continuity with corresponding interfaces of an adjacently stacked module upon engagement.

In a further aspect, at least one of the power transfer interface or data transfer interface comprises a retractable connector assembly, the retractable connector assembly being movable between a retracted position, in which a connector element is recessed within the housing to protect the connector element from contamination or mechanical damage, and an extended position, in which the connector element projects from the housing to engage a corresponding connector element of an adjacent module.

---

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION

### General Architecture

Referring generally to the figures, a rack module (100) is provided for use in a medical device administration system, the rack module (100) being configured for selective vertical stacking with one or more additional rack modules (100a, 100b, ... 100n) to form a modular administration rack assembly. Each rack module (100) comprises a housing (110) having a top surface (112), a bottom surface (114), and a plurality of side surfaces (116) extending therebetween. The housing (110) may further comprise mechanical alignment features (118), such as guide pins, mating rails, or complementary detent structures, configured to facilitate proper registration of adjacent modules during stacking and to resist lateral shear forces during use.

The rack module (100) houses therein at least one medical administration subsystem (120), which may include, without limitation, an infusion pump mechanism, a syringe driver mechanism, a sensor module, or a control module, the subsystem (120) being operatively coupled to the power transfer interface (130) and the data transfer interface (140) described in further detail below.

### Power Transfer Interface

The power transfer interface (130) is disposed proximate the top surface (112) and/or bottom surface (114) of the housing (110) and is configured to convey electrical power between the rack module (100) and an adjacently stacked module. In certain embodiments, the power transfer interface (130) comprises a first power connector (132) disposed at the bottom surface (114) and a second power connector (134) disposed at the top surface (112), the first power connector (132) and second power connector (134) being electrically coupled via an internal power bus (136) disposed within the housing (110).

In certain embodiments, the power transfer interface (130) further comprises power conditioning circuitry (138) configured to regulate, distribute, or isolate electrical power passed between stacked modules, such that a fault condition occurring in one module does not propagate to adjacently stacked modules. The power conditioning circuitry (138) may further comprise overcurrent protection, galvanic isolation, or redundant power pathways to enhance patient safety in accordance with applicable medical device electrical safety standards.

### Data Transfer Interface

The data transfer interface (140) is likewise disposed at the top surface (112) and/or bottom surface (114) of the housing (110) and is configured to enable bidirectional or unidirectional data communication between the rack module (100) and an adjacently stacked module. The data transfer interface (140) may implement any suitable communication protocol, including, without limitation, serial communication, a controller area network (CAN) protocol, or a proprietary medical device communication protocol, and may further comprise a data bus (146) disposed within the housing (110) and electrically coupled to a control circuit (150) of the medical administration subsystem (120).

In certain embodiments, the data transfer interface (140) is configured to convey identification information, operational status information, alarm condition information, or therapy parameter information between the rack module (100) and one or more adjacently stacked modules, thereby enabling coordinated operation of a plurality of rack modules (100) within a stacked assembly, such as synchronized dosing schedules, aggregated alarm reporting, or centralized system status display.

### Retractable Connector Assembly

In accordance with an aspect of the present disclosure, at least one of the power transfer interface (130) or the data transfer interface (140) comprises a retractable connector assembly (200). The retractable connector assembly (200) generally comprises a connector element (210), such as a pin header, blade contact, pogo-pin array, or other electrically conductive contact structure, mounted upon a carriage (220) configured for translational movement relative to the housing (110) between a retracted position and an extended position.

In the retracted position, the connector element (210) is recessed within a recess (230) formed in the top surface (112) or bottom surface (114) of the housing (110), such that the connector element (210) is substantially shielded from external contaminants, fluid ingress, or mechanical impact. In the extended position, the connector element (210) projects outwardly from the recess (230) beyond the plane of the top surface (112) or bottom surface (114) so as to establish physical and electrical contact with a corresponding connector element (210') of an adjacently stacked rack module (100a).

In certain embodiments, the carriage (220) is biased toward the retracted position by a biasing member (240), such as a compression spring, and is displaced toward the extended position in response to an actuation force. The actuation force may be provided by:

(a) **mechanical actuation**, wherein the act of stacking an adjacent module (100a) onto the rack module (100) causes a corresponding engagement feature (250) of the adjacent module (100a) to bear against an actuation surface (222) of the carriage (220), thereby displacing the carriage (220) toward the extended position;

(b) **motorized actuation**, wherein the rack module (100) further comprises an actuator (260), such as a solenoid, linear motor, or motor-driven lead screw, operatively coupled to the carriage (220) and configured to displace the carriage (220) between the retracted position and the extended position in response to a control signal generated by the control circuit (150); or

(c) **manual actuation**, wherein the housing (110) further comprises a manually operable control, such as a lever, slide, or push-button, operatively coupled to the carriage (220) and accessible from an exterior surface of the housing (110).

In certain embodiments, the retractable connector assembly (200) further comprises a sensor (270), such as a limit switch, hall-effect sensor, or optical sensor, configured to detect a position of the carriage (220) and to generate a signal indicative of the retracted position or the extended position, the signal being communicated to the control circuit (150) for the purpose of confirming successful engagement of the connector element (210) with the corresponding connector element (210') prior to the initiation of power transfer or data transfer therebetween.

In certain embodiments, the control circuit (150) is configured to withhold the initiation of power transfer or data transfer via the retractable connector assembly (200) until the sensor (270) confirms that the connector element (210) has reached the extended position and has established a validated connection with the corresponding connector element (210') of the adjacent module, thereby reducing the risk of arcing, partial engagement, or data corruption during the stacking process.

In certain embodiments, the retractable connector assembly (200) is further configured to automatically return the connector element (210) to the retracted position upon detection of a separation event between the rack module (100) and the adjacent module (100a), such as a physical decoupling of the housings (110) or an interruption in a continuity signal monitored by the control circuit (150), thereby protecting the connector element (210) from damage during module removal.

### Mechanical Interlocking and Alignment

The housing (110) may further comprise a locking mechanism (280), such as a latch, cam-lock, or quarter-turn fastener, configured to mechanically secure the rack module (100) to an adjacently stacked module and to prevent inadvertent separation during use. In certain embodiments, the locking mechanism (280) is operatively interlocked with the retractable connector assembly (200), such that the connector element (210) is permitted to transition to the extended position only when the locking mechanism (280) has achieved a fully secured state, and conversely, such that the locking mechanism (280) cannot be released until the connector element (210) has been returned to the retracted position, thereby providing a safety interlock that sequences mechanical and electrical engagement/disengagement operations.

### Exemplary Method of Operation

In one exemplary method of operation, a first rack module (100) is positioned in a stacking orientation relative to a second rack module (100a), such that the bottom surface (114) of the second rack module (100a) is brought into proximity with the top surface (112) of the first rack module (100). The mechanical alignment features (118) engage to register the modules (100, 100a) in a predetermined relative position. Continued relative motion of the modules (100, 100a) toward one another actuates the locking mechanism (280) toward a secured state and, either concurrently or subsequently, actuates the retractable connector assembly (200) from the retracted position to the extended position, thereby establishing electrical continuity between the power transfer interface (130) and data transfer interface (140) of the respective modules (100, 100a). The sensor (270) detects successful engagement and communicates a confirmation signal to the control circuit (150), which thereafter enables power transfer and data communication between the stacked modules (100, 100a).

---

## CLAIMS (Exemplary, Non-Limiting)

**1.** A rack module for a medical device administration system, comprising:
   a housing comprising a top surface and a bottom surface, the housing configured to be stacked with an adjacent rack module;
   a power transfer interface disposed at at least one of the top surface or the bottom surface;
   a data transfer interface disposed at at least one of the top surface or the bottom surface; and
   a retractable connector assembly associated with at least one of the power transfer interface or the data transfer interface, the retractable connector assembly comprising a connector element movable between a retracted position, in which the connector element is recessed within the housing, and an extended position, in which the connector element projects from the housing to engage a corresponding connector element of the adjacent rack module.

**2.** The rack module of claim 1, wherein the retractable connector assembly further comprises a carriage supporting the connector element and a biasing member configured to bias the carriage toward the retracted position.

**3.** The rack module of claim 1, further comprising a sensor configured to detect whether the connector element is in the extended position and to generate a signal indicative thereof.

**4.** The rack module of claim 3, further comprising a control circuit configured to withhold initiation of power transfer or data transfer via the retractable connector assembly until the signal indicates that the connector element has reached the extended position.

# Invention Summary: Stackable Rack System for Medical Administration Devices

## Field of the Invention

This invention relates generally to support and organizational systems for medical equipment, and more particularly to a stackable rack system configured to secure, organize, and interconnect medical administration devices—such as infusion pumps, syringe pumps, and related fluid or medication delivery apparatuses—in a modular, vertically or horizontally expandable arrangement.

## Background

Medical administration devices are frequently deployed in multiples at a single patient bedside or point of care, requiring secure mounting, efficient spatial organization, and reliable mechanical and/or electrical interconnection between units. Conventional rack and mounting solutions typically rely on fixed brackets, permanent hardware, or separate cabling harnesses to join adjacent device housings or rack modules. Such fixed-connection approaches present several drawbacks: they complicate the assembly and disassembly of stacked configurations, increase setup and breakdown time in clinical environments, risk damage to connection interfaces during transport, and often fail to accommodate variable numbers of devices without additional tools or hardware.

There exists a need for a rack system that allows individual rack units to be selectively and repeatably joined to and separated from adjacent units, while protecting the interconnection mechanism when not in use, and without requiring separate tools, fasteners, or cabling.

## Summary of the Invention

The present invention provides a stackable rack system for holding one or more medical administration devices, comprising a plurality of rack units each configured to removably receive and support at least one medical administration device, wherein adjacent rack units may be mechanically and/or electrically joined to one another via a movable connector assembly integrated into at least one rack unit.

In accordance with an aspect of the invention, each rack unit comprises a housing or frame defining a receiving region sized and configured to hold a medical administration device, and at least one connector member movably mounted to the housing, the connector member being displaceable between:

1. **a storage position**, in which the connector member is retracted, recessed, or otherwise disposed substantially within or flush against the housing so as to be protected from inadvertent contact, damage, or interference during handling, transport, or non-stacked use; and

2. **a connected position**, in which the connector member is extended, rotated, translated, or otherwise displaced outward from the housing so as to engage a corresponding mating structure on an adjacent rack unit, thereby mechanically coupling the two rack units and, in certain embodiments, establishing an electrical connection between them.

The connector member may be mounted for sliding, pivoting, rotating, or telescoping movement relative to the housing, and may be biased toward the storage position, the connected position, or a neutral intermediate position by a spring or other resilient biasing element. In certain embodiments, the connector member is manually actuated by a user via a lever, slide, button, or knob accessible on an exterior surface of the rack unit. In other embodiments, the connector member is configured to automatically transition from the storage position to the connected position upon detection of engagement with, or proximity to, an adjacent rack unit, such as via a cam surface, detent mechanism, or biasing element responsive to mechanical contact.

In certain embodiments, the connector member includes a mechanical coupling feature—such as a projection, hook, latch, dovetail, or interlocking tab—configured to engage a corresponding receiving feature on an adjacent rack unit, thereby providing structural stability to the stacked assembly and resisting separation, tipping, or shifting of joined units. In certain embodiments, the connector member additionally or alternatively includes one or more electrical contacts configured to align with and engage corresponding electrical contacts on an adjacent rack unit when the connector member is in the connected position, thereby establishing a data and/or power connection between rack units without the need for external cabling. Such electrical connection may facilitate shared power distribution, communication between administration devices, centralized monitoring, or software-based lockout or interlock features between adjacent units.

In further embodiments, the rack system includes a locking mechanism configured to retain the connector member in the connected position until intentionally released by a user, thereby preventing inadvertent separation of stacked units during use or transport. The locking mechanism may include a detent, latch, spring-loaded pin, or other releasable retention feature.

The rack units may be configured for stacking in a vertical orientation, a horizontal orientation, or a combination thereof, and the connector member(s) may be positioned on a top surface, bottom surface, side surface, or combination of surfaces of the rack unit housing to accommodate multi-directional stacking configurations. Multiple connector members may be provided on a single rack unit to permit simultaneous connection to more than one adjacent rack unit, enabling assembly of two-dimensional or three-dimensional arrays of interconnected rack units.

## Advantages of the Invention

The disclosed stackable rack system provides numerous advantages over conventional fixed-mount rack solutions, including but not limited to:

- **Tool-free assembly and disassembly** of stacked rack configurations, reducing setup time in clinical environments;
- **Protection of connection interfaces** during transport, storage, and non-stacked use, owing to the retractable storage position of the connector member;
- **Scalability**, allowing a variable number of rack units to be joined together based on the number of medical administration devices required at a given point of care;
- **Improved structural stability** of stacked assemblies through mechanical interlocking features;
- **Simplified electrical integration** between adjacent devices without separate cabling, where electrical connector features are included; and
- **Reduced risk of damage** to connection hardware compared to fixed or exposed connector designs.

## Brief Description of Alternative Embodiments

It is contemplated that the movable connector assembly described herein may be implemented using a variety of mechanical arrangements, including but not limited to sliding drawers, pivoting arms, rotating discs, telescoping rods, or magnetically-assisted sliding elements, without departing from the scope of the invention. Similarly, the medical administration devices supported by the rack units may include, without limitation, infusion pumps, syringe pumps, patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) pumps, enteral feeding pumps, or other fluid or medication delivery devices known in the art. The invention is not limited to the specific embodiments described herein, and it is intended that the appended claims cover all such modifications and embodiments as fall within the true spirit and scope of the invention.

# RACK MODULE FOR SUPPORTING MEDICAL DEVICES

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates generally to modular support systems for medical devices, and more particularly to rack modules configured for stacking arrangements that provide both mechanical interconnection and electrical continuity between adjacent modules, while also providing protective features for exposed electrical connectors during periods of non-stacked storage or transport.

## BACKGROUND

Medical environments, including hospitals, clinics, ambulatory care facilities, and emergency response settings, frequently require the use of multiple medical devices in combination, such as infusion pumps, patient monitors, ventilators, syringe pumps, and other therapeutic or diagnostic equipment. These devices are often mounted on rack systems, poles, or carts to facilitate organization, portability, and ease of access by clinical staff.

Conventional rack systems typically require separate power cabling and data cabling to be manually connected between each device and a central power source or network hub. This arrangement introduces several disadvantages, including cluttered cabling that may create tripping hazards or become entangled with other equipment, increased setup and teardown time for clinical staff, potential for improper connections leading to device malfunction, and difficulty in reconfiguring the number or arrangement of devices in response to changing patient needs.

Some existing modular rack systems attempt to address these issues by incorporating electrical pass-through connections between stacked modules. However, such systems often suffer from exposed connector contacts when modules are used individually or when a module is positioned at the top or bottom of a stack, leaving contacts vulnerable to contamination from bodily fluids, cleaning agents, dust, or moisture—all of particular concern in medical settings where infection control and device reliability are paramount. Exposed contacts may also be susceptible to physical damage, electrical shorting, or accidental contact by personnel, creating potential safety hazards.

There remains a need for a rack module system that provides reliable mechanical and electrical interconnection between stacked modules while also protecting exposed connector interfaces during storage, transport, or standalone use.

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The present invention provides a rack module for supporting medical devices, wherein the module is configured to mechanically and electrically interconnect with one or more additional, substantially identical rack modules in a stacked configuration. Each rack module comprises a housing having a top surface and a bottom surface, the housing being configured to support a medical device or to be stacked with other rack modules to form a rack assembly.

The rack module includes a first electrical connector disposed on the top surface of the housing and a second electrical connector disposed on the bottom surface of the housing, the first and second connectors being electrically coupled to one another via internal wiring or a circuit board disposed within the housing. When two rack modules are stacked such that the bottom surface of an upper module engages the top surface of a lower module, the first electrical connector of the lower module mates with the second electrical connector of the upper module, thereby establishing an electrical connection that allows power and/or data signals to pass between the stacked modules without the need for external cabling.

The housing further comprises one or more mechanical alignment or locking features, such as guide pins, recesses, latches, or complementary interlocking geometries, disposed on the top and bottom surfaces, which cooperate with corresponding features on adjacent modules to secure the modules together in the stacked configuration and to ensure proper alignment of the electrical connectors during mating.

According to a further aspect of the invention, the rack module includes a protective cover or cap configured to selectively shield one of the electrical connectors—for example, the connector disposed on the bottom surface of the housing—when the module is used independently or is positioned at the bottom of a stack such that the connector would otherwise remain exposed. The protective cover may be hingedly attached, slidably attached, or removably attached to the housing, and may be biased toward a closed or protective position by a spring or other biasing member, such that the cover automatically moves to expose the connector when the module is stacked upon another module, and automatically returns to a protective position when the module is removed from the stack.

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION

### General Configuration

Referring generally to the rack module of the present disclosure, the module comprises a housing formed of a rigid or semi-rigid material suitable for medical environments, such as molded plastic, powder-coated metal, or a composite material resistant to common disinfectants and cleaning agents used in healthcare settings. The housing defines a generally rectangular, tray-like, or shelf-like structure having a top surface configured to receive and support a medical device thereon, and a bottom surface configured to rest upon or engage an adjacent rack module or a base unit, such as a pole clamp, cart mount, or wall mount.

The housing may further include side walls, a rear panel, or a front panel configured to provide structural support, to house internal electrical components, and/or to provide a mounting interface for accessories such as cable management clips, device retention straps, or auxiliary brackets.

### Electrical Interconnection Between Stacked Modules

The rack module includes a first electrical connector positioned at or near the top surface of the housing and a second electrical connector positioned at or near the bottom surface of the housing, the first and second connectors being of complementary type such that the first connector of one module is configured to mechanically and electrically mate with the second connector of an adjacent module when the modules are stacked in a vertical or substantially vertical arrangement.

In one embodiment, the first electrical connector comprises a plurality of exposed contact pins, pogo pins, or spring-loaded contacts, and the second electrical connector comprises a corresponding plurality of contact pads, sockets, or receptacles configured to receive the pins or contacts of the first connector. In an alternative embodiment, both the first and second connectors may comprise blind-mate connectors, such as pogo-pin-to-pad interfaces, magnetic pogo connectors, or multi-pin board-to-board connectors, configured to establish a reliable electrical connection upon the application of a stacking force, without requiring precise manual alignment by the user.

The first and second electrical connectors are electrically coupled to one another within the housing via internal wiring, a flexible printed circuit, or a rigid printed circuit board assembly disposed within an internal cavity of the housing. This internal coupling establishes a continuous electrical pass-through path such that power received at the second connector (e.g., from a module below) is passed through the module to the first connector (e.g., to a module above), and similarly for data or communication signals. In some embodiments, the internal circuitry may further include power conditioning components, such as voltage regulators, fuses, or surge protection elements, and/or data processing components, such as a microcontroller configured to manage communication protocols, perform module identification or addressing, or monitor the status of the electrical connection.

In embodiments incorporating data communication, the electrical connectors may be configured to carry both power and data signals via a shared multi-pin interface, or the module may include separate dedicated connectors for power and data, respectively, each having a complementary pair disposed on the top and bottom surfaces of the housing.

The pass-through electrical architecture enables a stack of any desired number of rack modules to be electrically connected to a single power source and/or data source connected to the bottommost or topmost module in the stack, without requiring individual cabling to each module. This significantly reduces cable clutter and setup complexity in clinical environments where multiple devices must be rapidly deployed or reconfigured.

### Mechanical Interconnection Between Stacked Modules

In addition to the electrical interconnection described above, the rack module comprises one or more mechanical coupling features configured to physically secure adjacent modules together when stacked, thereby preventing unintended separation, shifting, or misalignment of the modules and their respective electrical connectors during use, transport, or in response to vibration or impact.

In one embodiment, the top surface of the housing includes one or more alignment pins, protrusions, or raised bosses, and the bottom surface of the housing includes corresponding recesses, apertures, or sockets configured to receive the alignment features of an adjacent module when stacked. The engagement of the alignment features serves to guide the modules into proper registration such that the first and second electrical connectors are correctly aligned for mating, and further resists lateral or rotational displacement of the stacked modules relative to one another.

In a further embodiment, the rack module includes one or more mechanical latches, clips, or locking tabs disposed on the housing, configured to engage complementary latch-receiving features on an adjacent module so as to releasably lock the modules together in the stacked configuration. The latch mechanism may be manually actuated (e.g., via a button, lever, or slide) or may be configured to automatically engage upon stacking, such as via a spring-loaded detent mechanism, and may further include a release mechanism to permit intentional separation of the modules by clinical or technical personnel.

The combination of the alignment features and the latch or locking features ensures that the mechanical connection between stacked modules is robust and reliable, while also ensuring that the electrical connectors remain properly mated and are not subjected to undue mechanical stress, shear force, or repeated micro-movement that could degrade the electrical connection over time or lead to connector wear.

### Connector Protection Feature for Storage and Standalone Use

A particular feature of the rack module addresses the issue of connector exposure when a module is used independently (i.e., not stacked with any other module) or when a module is positioned such that one of its electrical connectors—typically the connector disposed on the bottom surface of the housing—is not mated with an adjacent module and would otherwise remain exposed to the external environment.

In one embodiment, the rack module includes a protective cover configured to selectively enclose or shield the second electrical connector (e.g., the bottom connector) when the module is not stacked beneath another module. The protective cover may take the form of a hinged flap, sliding door, rotatable shutter, or removable cap, disposed on or adjacent to the bottom surface of the housing, and configured to move between a first, protective position in which the electrical connector is substantially enclosed and shielded from environmental exposure, and a second, retracted position in which the electrical connector is exposed and available for mating with an adjacent module.

In a preferred embodiment, the protective cover is biased toward the protective position by a biasing member, such as a coil spring, torsion spring, or resilient elastomeric element, such that the cover automatically returns to the protective position when the module is removed from a stack or is otherwise not engaged with an adjacent module. When the rack module is stacked upon another module, the top surface of the lower module (or a corresponding actuation feature thereon) contacts the protective cover of the upper module and displaces it from the protective position to the retracted position against the force of the biasing member, thereby exposing the second electrical connector and permitting it to mate with the first electrical connector of the lower module. Upon separation of the modules, the biasing member urges the protective cover back to the protective position, automatically re-shielding the second electrical connector.

In alternative embodiments, the protective cover may be manually actuated by the user, for example via a slide latch or a rotatable dial, allowing the user to selectively expose or shield the connector as needed. In still further embodiments, the protective cover may comprise a resilient flexible membrane or gasket configured to be pierced or displaced by the mating connector of an adjacent module upon stacking, while returning to a sealed configuration upon separation of the modules, thereby providing a degree of liquid or particulate ingress protection to the connector even during transitions between stacked and standalone states.

The protective cover may further be configured to provide a substantially flush or contoured exterior surface when in the protective position, such that the bottom surface of the housing presents a smooth, cleanable exterior suitable for wipe-down disinfection procedures commonly employed in medical environments. The materials used for the protective cover may include antimicrobial or disinfectant-resistant plastics or coatings, consistent with infection control requirements applicable to medical device accessories.

It will be appreciated that while the foregoing description references a protective cover disposed on the bottom surface of the housing, in alternative embodiments the protective cover may be disposed on the top surface of the housing, or protective covers may be provided on both the top and bottom surfaces of the housing, depending on the intended orientation of use and the configuration of the r
